'''Charon Robin Ganellin''' (25 January 1934 – 27 June 2026) was a British medicinal chemist and Smith Kline and French Professor of Medicinal Chemistry, at [[University College London]].<ref>[https://iris.ucl.ac.uk/research/personal?upi=CRGAN19 Profile], ucl.ac.uk. Accessed 13 April 2024.</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Ganellin |first1=C. Robin |title=Professor C. Robin Ganellin FRS |journal=J. Chem. Soc., Perkin Trans. 1 |date=2001 |volume=13 |issue=13 |page=i |doi=10.1039/B101382N |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2001/P1/b101382n|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Ganellin contributed much to the field of drug discovery and development. He was involved in the development of [[cimetidine]], a drug used to combat stomach ulcers, when working at [[Smith Kline and French]] which he stated was the achievement in which he took the most pride.<ref name="Ganellin, C. Robin 2004, p158">Ganellin, C. Robin. Drug Discovery Today, Feb 2004, Vol. 9 Issue 4, p158, 3p</ref>

==Early life==
Ganellin was born in East London. His father and maternal uncle were chemists, which influenced his choice of profession despite a stated interest in biology and natural history.<ref name="Ganellin, C. Robin 2004, p158" /> As a child, Ganellin studied at Harrow County Grammar School.<ref name=":0" /> He began his formal studies at [[Queen Mary, University of London|Queen Mary College]] in London where he received his bachelor of science in chemistry.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Emeritus Fellow - Prof. C. Robin Ganellin |url=https://iupac.org/who-we-are/divisions/vii-emeritus-fellows/emeritus-fellow-prof-c-robin-ganellin/ |access-date=26 February 2025 |website=IUPAC {{!}} International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry |language=en-US}}</ref> Ganellin continued studying at [[Queen Mary, University of London|Queen Mary College]] researching [[tropylium]] chemistry with Michael J.S. Dewar where he discovered how to isolate the tropylium cation from cyclooctatetraene. Ganellin was awarded his PhD in organic chemistry in 1958 at age 24 for defending his dissertation titled "Studies in the tropylium series."<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Ganellin |first=Charon Robin |title=Studies in the tropylium series |date=1958 |url=https://search.library.qmul.ac.uk/iii/encore/record/C__Rb1171599?lang=eng&ivts=dsUmkG8%2Bk1pYs%2FCffvplTA%3D%3D&casts=EtV%2Ba0965Xeo5YmF%2BRyphA%3D%3D}}</ref>

==Scientific work==
In 1958, shortly after his PhD studies at Queen Mary College, Ganellin joined Smith Kline and French Laboratories in the UK where he began research in medicinal chemistry.<ref name="Ganellin, C. Robin 2004, p158"/> Two years after starting at SK&F, he went to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] where he performed his postdoctoral work with Arthur C. Cope. At MIT, he devised the first direct optical resolution of a chiral [[olefin]] using platinum complex chemistry. After a year at MIT, he returned to the UK to resume his work at SK&F. In 1966, he headed a landmark research team at SK&F, collaborating with [[James Black (pharmacologist)|James Black]] researching histamine [[H2-receptor antagonists]]. This research eventually led to the discovery of [[Cimetidine]], also known by its trademark name Tagamet which is currently produced by GlaxoSmith Kline. Cimetidine quickly garnered over one billion dollars in annual sales.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.guernicamag.com/features/111/me_too_drugs/ |title=Pharmaceutical Sales 101: Me-Too Drugs by Jake Whitney – Guernica / A Magazine of Art & Politics |access-date=3 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080807114344/http://www.guernicamag.com/features/111/me_too_drugs/ |archive-date=7 August 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Awards and achievements==
Ganellin authored or co-authored over 260 scientific papers and is listed as inventor or co-inventor on over 160 US patents.<ref name=":1" /> He served as the president of the [[IUPAC]] medicinal chemistry section, and for 10 years (until 2012) he was the chair of the subcommittee on medicinal chemistry and drug development. He won many awards and commendations, both for his work on cimetidine and his research in other areas of medicinal chemistry. He received awards in medicinal chemistry from many organisations, such as the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]], the [[American Chemical Society]], the [[Society of Chemical Industry]], the Society for Drug Research, the European Federation for Medicinal Chemistry, the Société Chimie Thérapeutique of France, and the Medicinal Chemistry Division of the [[Italian Chemical Society]].

He was also inducted into the US [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]] in 1990 for his work on cimetidine. 

==Death==

Ganellin died on 27 June 2026, at the age of 92.<ref>[https://www.thetimes.com/comment/register/article/births-marriages-and-deaths-july-11-2026-092r9zc5d Ganellin]</ref>
